newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-TIGER BURNS BRIGHT IN STAR TURN AT MASTERS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-TIGER BURNS BRIGHT IN STAR TURN AT MASTERS.

text.p: The future has arrived in golf. His name is Tiger and he burned brighter than any star ever at the Masters.

Tiger Woods is no longer the whispered about next great player. He turned the whispers into roars with a devastating performance in his first major as a pro that had wisened veterans of the Augusta National wars dropping their jaws in wonder.
U.S. Ryder Cup captain Tom Kite, winner of the 1992 U.S. Open, finished second a dozen shots behind 21-year-old Woods.

Kite, who has played in 24 Masters, suggested the green jacketed folks consider a few changes such as lengthening the course, adding sand traps or growing rough to neutralise the new kid on the block.
Woods set the Masters scoring record, won by the biggest margin ever and became the first player of colour to win a major championship all in one fell swoop on Sunday.
Did we mention he was the youngest player ever to win in 61 Masters?
Woods wowed them with such power off the tee that he was routinely hitting wedge shots into par-5s. Sometimes he took it easy off the tee and used a 3-wood, eight-iron combination.
The kid can putt, too. Remember how ridiculously unfair the greens were in Thursday's first round?
Well, after scuffling around the front nine in an untidy 40, Woods gave himself a talking to and then posted a 30 on the back half, one shot off the last nine record.
Some players feel it's unfair to allow Woods to play the Masters on the same course that Bobby Jones, Byron Nelson, Sam Snead, Ben Hogan, Arnold Palmer and Jack Nicklaus battled on.
Sweden's Jesper Parnevik, who shot a respectable one-over 289 to tie for 21st in his first Masters, had a suggestion.

"They may have to have Tiger tees here. If they don't move the tees back 50 yards for him, he might win the next 20 Masters," said Parnevik, who could end up squinting down the fairway at Woods in the Ryder Cup later this year.
Kite contended something should be done but wasn't sure what.

"Obviously, the Masters committee has to be a little concerned," said Kite. "They've got a golf course that's pretty darn tough, and they've got somebody just ripping it. So what are they going to do to make this course more difficult?

"They certainly could not get the greens any faster. They could not get them any harder than they were in the first day. They could not get any more severe pin placements. So what defence does this golf course have other than tightening up somehow?"
Twice champion Tom Watson, who was fourth, 14 strokes back of Woods, rebutted Kite's comments.

"Leave it alone. Let's see what this young man can do. Why make it more difficult? Let's see how it stands throughout time. Let's see how good this kid is," he said. "He may win 10 Masters like Jack Nicklaus said he might. He may be the type of player that comes around once in a millennium. Let's compare."
Watson likes Woods's competitive makeup.
"He's obviously a winner. He's won everything in amateur golf there is to win in this country," said Watson, referring to his three junior amateur and three U.S. Amateur titles.

"When you have that type of attitude about winning, like when he said 'second place sucks' after finishing second (when a stirring comeback at Pebble Beach fell short). That tells you something about the young man. He's got the heart of a lion. He's got whatever it takes."
Woods believes a Grand Slam is possible.
"I think it can be done," he said. "If you win the right four tournaments then you have the slam." Woods has won four tournaments in 15 starts as a professional.
Woods did not shy away when asked if he thought he was going to be the greatest player the world had ever seen.

"I don't know about that, but I know my goal is to obviously be the best. I know that's a lofty goal, but I think that if I try to accomplish that goal, if I do, great. If I don't, I tried. I expect nothing but the best for myself."
Last year, Nick Faldo swiped the green jacket from Greg Norman, playing a brilliant final round while the Australian lost touch with his golf game and blew a six-shot lead.
After that cataclysmic Masters Sunday round, Faldo gave Norman "the hug felt round the world."
Norman, by the way, was so shattered he spent a day with a motivational cable TV self-improvement guru to refresh his confidence just before coming to Augusta last week. He missed the cut.
In what seemed like the continuance of a Masters tradition, Tiger Woods walked straight to his father Earl after his last putt and engaged in a long embrace, wiping a tear from his eye after parting.
Asked about their hug, Earl Woods said: "I said, 'We did it. I love you and I'm so proud of you.'"
The only criticism of Woods came from outgoing champion Faldo, who, upon helping the young American into the coveted green jacket, chided him for wearing a clashing red golf shirt.
Woods won that exchange as well.
"Mom believes that red is my power colour," he told Faldo, who also missed the cut after shooting 81 on Friday. "I always do what Mama says."
